metadata.file_name: Epistemic beliefs in science  socio-economic status  and mathematics and science test results in lower secondary education  a multilevel perspective.pdf
metadata.title: Epistemic beliefs in science socio-economic status and mathematics and science test results in lower secondary education a multilevel perspective

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 Estonia microdata with a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools sampled first, then students within schools), where sampling weights are required due to unequal selection probabilities. For multilevel models, the authors report using non-response adjusted school base weights (as recommended in Mang et al., 2021) rather than only student weights, to improve accuracy in nested models. The analysis pools estimates across the 10 plausible values using Rubins (1987) multiple-imputation approach implemented via mitml, which is consistent with complex survey handling for PV-based achievement outcomes. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty quantification is described through standard errors from the multilevel estimation and pooling rather than explicit replicate variance estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample is restricted to the PISA 2015 Estonia dataset and includes only 9th grade students for comparability. Participants without achievement test scores were excluded, and cases with missing values on more than two epistemic beliefs in science (EBS) items were removed. After these exclusions, less than 0.5% missing data remained and were imputed using predictive mean matching. Finally, students were excluded from schools with fewer than 10 students, yielding the effective sample of 3991 students from 81 schools.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level regression (pooled across 10 PVs): total R2 = 0.175. Key pooled unstandardised effects: Gender (boys vs girls) = -7.44 (SE 3.04, p = .018); Student SES = 25.86 (SE 2.02, p < .001); Student EBS = 23.05 (SE 1.65, p < .001); School SES = 24.50 (SE 9.22, p = .008); School EBS = 18.26 (SE 11.97, p = .127).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Estonia Grade 9 Mathematics the study leveraged Gender, Student SES (ESCS), Student EBS (science), and School SES (ESCS) (with School EBS included) to predict Mathematics test score (PISA PVs), finding that higher student and school SES and higher student EBS were associated with higher mathematics scores, while school-level EBS was not statistically significant. This indicates that strengthening students science-related epistemic beliefs and addressing socioeconomic disparities at both student and school levels may be more actionable for improving mathematics performance than focusing solely on school-level epistemic-belief climate, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-level regression (pooled across 10 PVs): total R2 = 0.181. Key pooled unstandardised effects: Gender (boys vs girls) = -6.11 (SE 2.82, p = .031); Student SES = 24.29 (SE 1.90, p < .001); Student EBS = 29.98 (SE 1.64, p < .001); School SES = 22.96 (SE 9.90, p = .020); School EBS = 25.96 (SE 12.42, p = .037).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Estonia Grade 9 Science the study leveraged Gender, Student SES (ESCS), Student EBS (science), and School SES (ESCS) (with School EBS included) to predict Science test score (PISA PVs), finding that both student-level and school-level EBS and SES significantly predicted higher science scores, alongside higher student EBS and SES. This indicates that policies and school practices that foster more mature epistemic beliefs about science (e.g., evidence-based inquiry and justification practices) may help improve science achievement, particularly when supported by broader socioeconomic resources, though causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional multilevel associations.

data.outcome_summary: This study conducts a secondary analysis of PISA 2015 Estonia (Grade 9; 3991 students from 81 schools) to examine how epistemic beliefs in science (EBS) and socio-economic status (SES; ESCS) relate to mathematics and science achievement. The authors use two-level regression models with school as a random effect and pool estimates across the 10 plausible values using Rubins multiple-imputation approach. For mathematics, the pooled total R2 is 0.175; student SES and student EBS are significant positive predictors, school SES is significant, and school EBS is not significant (p = .127). For science, the pooled total R2 is 0.181; both student and school EBS and SES significantly predict higher science scores. Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal identification) and the possibility of partial conceptual overlap between the EBS questionnaire and science achievement content.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification study; it uses multilevel regression models and weighted correlations rather than training ML algorithms. Therefore, ml_techniques are left empty and primary is null, while the substantive results are reported as multilevel regression effects pooled across plausible values.
